newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore refiners see better margins as crude dips.
newsitem.headline: Singapore refiners see better margins as crude dips.

text.p: Singapore refiners are enjoying better refining profits, underpinned by lower crude prices and continued strength of oil product prices, but they remain unsure how long the upturn will last, refining sources said on Tuesday.
Refiners said they fear profits would come under pressure again if product prices eventually dip along with the fall in crude values, unless a cold winter props up North Asian demand.

Over the past month, strong regional prices of diesel, jet-kerosene fuel, fuel oil and naphtha have also encouraged Singapore's four refineries to restore crude runs to nearly full capacity of 1.2 million barrels-per-day (bpd), they said.
Only Shell Singapore, a unit of the Royal Dutch Shell Group, is shutting down its 35,000-bpd residue catalytic cracker for five-week scheduled maintenance from November 1.

Singapore refiners cut third quarter production in response to meagre refining margins since mid-year. Margins remained in the red in July despite a drop in crude prices at that time because oil product values also fell in line.

Currently, margins for primary refining -- the first stage of crude refining -- for Dubai crude hover at around $1.00 a barrel, compared with between breakeven and a 50-cent loss in late September to early October, the sources said.
Secondary margins are now around $2.00-$2.50 a barrel, they said. "We are seeing an improvement but we are not sure how long it will hold, " one refiner said.
"Spot product prices are now quite healthy but they might dip slightly at a later stage. No one is quite sure how Northeast Asian demand would be although people are anticipating a mild winter."
The international benchmark Brent crude price has plunged to a current $22.25 from its five-year peak of $25.06 a barrel on October 15.

Asian benchmark Tapis, which has been sustained at high levels because of the strength of diesel and jet-kerosene fuel prices, also slid to $24.90 for December deliveries from its mid-October high of $25.75.
Some traders said Asian crudes could soon face more pressure because lower Brent prices make it economical to ship West African crudes eastward.
Dubai, the most-widely used crude in Singapore, is assessed at $20.30, down from $22.09 in mid-October.
Meanwhile, diesel and jet-kerosene fuel prices have gained about 50 cents a barrel from mid-October to over $30.
Traders said diesel prices are supported from Indonesia, China and India, while jet fuel prices have been held up by Indonesian demand.
But as heating oil prices come under pressure, the eventual flow of diesel and jet fuel cargoes from the United States, Mediterranean and Europe to Asia could dampen Singapore prices.
The fuel oil market is pressured by ample supplies and weak demand, but is being supported at over $116 per tonne by the forward swaps market.
Naphtha prices also remained strong around $23.00 as demand is expected to pick up with new petrochemical plants coming up in Thailand, India, Singapore and Indonesia.
But gasoline is under pressure due to abundant supplies as new refining capacities come onstream in China, Thailand and South Korea, as well as from competition from Russian leaded gasoline.
Gasoline demand is growing at a slower pace compared with supplies and prices remained constant below $25.00 per barrel.
